title: Conventional FP16 Mixed-Precision Training
question: How does conventional FP16 training preserve an FP32 update path?
scope: This is one conventional recipe; frameworks vary, and BF16 commonly omits loss scaling.

steps.title: Keep the master copy
steps.description: FP32 Master Weights are cast for FP16 computation. The lower-precision weights serve the forward path while the master copy supports the later update.

steps.title: Scale before backward
steps.description: The forward path produces a loss; Step 3 scales it before backpropagation. The scaled FP16 gradient path helps avoid losing small gradient values.

steps.title: Unscale before updating
steps.description: Step 5 copies and unscales gradients into the FP32 path. Only then does Step 6 update the FP32 master weights, preserving the meaning of the optimizer step.

review_notes: Inspected canonical rendered artwork from /tmp/mlsys-figure-art/index.json; mapped original labeled objects and panels. No geometry or evidence altered.

title: Gradient Accumulation
question: How can several micro-batches contribute to one optimizer update?
scope: Apply consistent loss normalization; batch-dependent layers and randomness can prevent exact equivalence to a single larger batch.

steps.title: Keep each micro-batch distinct
steps.description: Batch 1, Batch 2, and Batch 3 each produce a loss. Sequential micro-batches can reuse sample and activation storage rather than holding the whole logical batch at once.

steps.title: Accumulate parameter gradients
steps.description: Each loss produces its own gradient tensor. Parameters remain fixed while these contributions accumulate for the same logical optimizer step.

steps.title: Update after combining
steps.description: The Sum box combines g₁, g₂, and g₃ for one update. Scale or average consistently with the intended loss; accumulation reduces sample residency, not persistent model or optimizer state.

title: Data Parallelism
question: What is replicated and what is synchronized in data parallel training?
scope: This is logical synchronous data parallelism; communication overlap and exact averaging rules are implementation-specific.

steps.title: Shard examples, replicate the model
steps.description: Input Data splits into four batches. Each GPU performs forward and backward computation with a complete model copy, so this strategy does not shrink the model state required per replica.

steps.title: Combine gradients
steps.description: Gradient Sync / AllReduce aggregates local gradient contributions across workers. Correct scaling is required to implement the intended global-batch objective.

steps.title: Keep replicas aligned
steps.description: The Model Update uses the synchronized gradient so replicas can proceed from matching parameters. Communication, input supply, and imbalance limit how close throughput gets to linear scaling.

title: Model Parallelism

steps.title: Distribute the layers

steps.title: Follow boundary activations

steps.title: Return boundary gradients

title: Layer-Wise Model Partitioning
question: Why does layerwise partitioning leave devices waiting for one micro-batch?
scope: The diagram allocates contiguous blocks; it does not include a micro-batch pipeline schedule.

steps.title: Read the allocation
steps.description: The 24 blocks are divided into four contiguous six-block partitions. This spreads layer storage across GPUs rather than replicating all layers everywhere.

steps.title: Follow the dependency
steps.description: Activations cross each boundary from one partition to the next. For a single micro-batch, Device 2 waits for Device 1’s boundary result, and later devices wait in turn.

steps.title: Separate capacity from utilization
steps.description: Device 4 enables the final partition to fit, but a four-device placement alone does not create four independent simultaneous computations. Improving utilization needs an explicit schedule such as micro-batch pipelining.

title: The D·A·M Axis Triad

steps.title: Locate the binding axis

title: Storage Layouts
question: How can a column-oriented layout avoid irrelevant field reads?
scope: This is the illustrated Age projection. Real savings depend on file format, compression, query planning, and physical I/O.

steps.title: Read whole records
steps.description: The Row-Oriented (CSV) strip interleaves ID, Age, and Loc for each record. The depicted scan reads all these fields even though only Age is requested.

steps.title: Group values by feature
steps.description: The Column-Oriented (Parquet) block groups both Age values together. Projection can request that chunk without reading the ID and Loc chunks shown around it.

steps.title: Connect layout to traffic
steps.description: The lower scan reads ONLY Age in this example. This reduces irrelevant movement for this query; it does not imply every query favors column storage or that bytes saved equal proportional speedup.

title: The Roofline Model
question: How does arithmetic intensity determine the relevant hardware ceiling?
scope: The schematic has no calibrated workload coordinates; a ceiling bounds attainable performance rather than guaranteeing it.

steps.title: Count computation per byte
steps.description: Arithmetic Intensity is FLOP/byte. Moving right means more arithmetic for the bytes moved, for example through data reuse rather than simply adding operations without a purpose.

steps.title: Read the bandwidth ceiling
steps.description: Left of the ridge, available memory bandwidth determines the sloped ceiling. Reducing memory traffic can increase the achievable bound in this regime.

steps.title: Meet the compute ceiling
steps.description: At the Ridge Point, the two limits meet. Beyond it, the flat compute ceiling applies; more reuse alone cannot exceed the peak arithmetic rate.

title: The Memory Hierarchy
question: Why stage data near computation instead of reading everything from storage?
scope: The pyramid is qualitative. Access ratios in the caption are illustrative; tier access costs depend on the platform and operation.

steps.title: Start from capacity
steps.description: Storage forms the broad base, with HBM/DRAM above it. Lower tiers provide larger capacity at lower cost but do not offer the lowest access latency.

steps.title: Stage for reuse
steps.description: Caches and registers sit closer to arithmetic. Reusing staged values avoids repeatedly paying a lower-tier access cost, while their limited capacity constrains what can remain resident.

steps.title: Balance both directions
steps.description: The side arrows oppose capacity and cost against speed and latency. A hierarchy works because no single medium supplies every desired property at once.

title: Numerical Format Bit Layouts
question: How do the numerical formats allocate bits differently?
scope: Bit width alone does not determine numerical quality, actual throughput, or total memory use; INT8 is not floating point.

steps.title: Read the FP32 reference
steps.description: FP32 allocates a sign bit, eight exponent bits, and 23 mantissa bits. The colored fields separate range-related exponent allocation from precision-related mantissa allocation.

steps.title: Compare equal-width formats
steps.description: BF16 and FP16 both use 16 bits but partition them differently. BF16 retains the eight-bit exponent field; FP16 uses five exponent bits and ten mantissa bits.

steps.title: Separate integer quantization
steps.description: INT8 is an eight-bit integer field, not a shorter floating-point exponent/mantissa split. Mapping real-valued tensors into it requires quantization scale and related metadata outside this raw layout.
